issues.legal_issue: A party cannot obtain restitution of possession from a former possessor when the estate and the right to recover possession have vested in the State, which is deemed to have taken charge.
material_facts: The plaintiffs took possession under a High Court decree that was later reversed.
Before the restitution claim, the estate containing the lands had vested in the State, and the Collector was deemed to have taken charge of it from the date of vesting.

The earlier title proceedings had held that the plaintiffs had no subsisting right to recover possession and that the right to possession and to recover possession from a trespasser had vested in the State.
The State was not a party to the earlier title proceedings, but later asserted that the plaintiffs had surrendered possession to it; the plaintiffs also said they had surrendered possession.
issues.conclusion: The defendants were not entitled to restitution of possession from the plaintiffs because the State, rather than either litigating party, held the right to possession after vesting.
issues.legal_principle: Section 144 CPC ordinarily provides restitution when a decree under which a party obtained a benefit is reversed, but that ordinary rule did not apply where Sections 3 and 4(a) of the Bihar Lands Reforms Act vested the estate and unsaved interests in the State, and Section 4(f) deemed the Collector to have taken charge from the date of vesting. The Court relied on its earlier decision in Surajnath Ahir v. Prithinath Singh, which held that the former proprietors had no subsisting right to recover possession after vesting and that the right to possession and recovery from a trespasser vested in the State.

rule.if: restitution_proceeding_after_reversal and estate_rights_vested_in_state and state_deemed_in_charge and claimant_has_no_surviving_right_to_possession

predicates.restitution_proceeding_after_reversal: A party seeks restitution of possession after a decree under which another party took possession has been reversed.
predicates.estate_rights_vested_in_state: The estate containing the disputed property and the relevant rights have vested in the State.
predicates.state_deemed_in_charge: The governing law deems the State's officer to have taken charge of the vested estate from the date of vesting.
predicates.claimant_has_no_surviving_right_to_posse: The party seeking restitution has no surviving right to possess the property or recover it from its possessor.

issues.definition: When a reversed-decree restitution proceeding concerns property whose rights have vested in the State, the State is deemed in charge, and the claimant has no surviving right to possession, the former possessor need not restore possession to that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: A party who is not entitled to restitution of possession because the right to possession belongs to the State is also not entitled to mesne profits for the period of exclusion.
material_facts: The defendants sought mesne profits for the period after the plaintiffs took possession under the subsequently reversed decree.
The estate had vested in the State before that period, and the Collector was deemed to have taken charge of it from the date of vesting.
The defendants were not entitled to restitution of possession from the plaintiffs.
issues.conclusion: The defendants were not entitled to mesne profits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 144 CPC in light of the vesting provisions in Sections 3 and 4 of the Bihar Lands Reforms Act. Because the defendants had no right to restitution of possession after the estate and the relevant rights vested in the State, they could not recover mesne profits on the same basis.

predicates.mesne_profits_claim_in_restitution_proce: A party claims mesne profits in a proceeding seeking restitution after reversal of a decree.
predicates.claimant_not_entitled_to_restitution: The party claiming mesne profits is not entitled to restitution of possession.

issues.definition: When a party claims mesne profits in a restitution proceeding but is not entitled to restitution, that party is not entitled to mesne profits.

issues.legal_issue: A decree or order in a proceeding concerning a vested estate is not binding on the State when the required notice of the proceeding has not been served on it.
material_facts: The estate had vested in the State while the title appeal was pending.
The State was not notified of, or made a party to, the title appeal, the appeal to the Supreme Court, or the initial restitution proceeding.
The State later sought to be added as a party and asserted its rights in the appeal concerning restitution.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decrees and orders were not binding on the State because the State had not been served with the required notice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(ee) of the Bihar Lands Reforms Act requires notice to the State in a pending suit, appeal, or proceeding concerning an estate vested under the Act; the State may apply to be added as a party, and in the absence of service of notice a decree or order is not binding on it. The Court noted that the State had no opportunity to present its objections in the earlier proceedings.

predicates.pending_proceeding_concerning_vested_est: A suit, appeal, or other proceeding concerning an estate is pending after the estate has vested in the State.
predicates.state_not_served_with_required_notice: The State is not served with the notice required for that proceeding.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerning an estate vested in the State is pending and the State is not served with the required notice, an order or decree in that proceeding is not binding on the State.

issues.legal_issue: Costs collected under the title-suit proceedings remained refundable even though restitution of possession and mesne profits were denied.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had collected costs from the defendants in the title-suit proceedings.
The plaintiffs did not resist the defendants' claim for refund of those costs.
The High Court had allowed the refund, and the Supreme Court left that part of the order undisturbed.
issues.conclusion: The order requiring the plaintiffs to refund the collected costs remained in force.
issues.legal_principle: The Court left the costs-refund order undisturbed because the claim had not been resisted; it did not set out a separate substantive rule beyond confirming that part of the order.

predicates.costs_collected_under_title_suit_decree: One party collected costs from another under the proceedings in the title suit.
predicates.refund_claim_uncontested: The party from whom refund is sought did not resist the claim for refund.

issues.definition: When costs were collected under the title-suit proceedings and the refund claim is uncontested, the collected costs must be refunded.
